text: PD falls have multiple contributors: postural instability and gait dysfunction, including freezing, matter, and orthostatic hypotension can cause dizziness, syncope or unexplained falls. A fall assessment should therefore consider blood-pressure-related causes as well as mobility. (medium confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: A small prospective observational study of 30 people with PD found fewer outdoor falls and fall injuries among rollator users. Participants used rollators only outdoors, and the study could not adjust for other factors because of its small sample; it does not establish causal protection, indoor benefit or superiority of a particular model. (low confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: Orthostatic-hypotension assessment includes blood-pressure measurements supine and after three minutes standing, plus assessment of possible causes such as hypovolemia or blood-pressure-lowering drugs. This is relevant when falls are unexplained or accompanied by standing-related symptoms. (low confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: In the PDSAFE randomized trial, the programme did not reduce falling overall, despite improvements in balance, falls efficacy and chair-stand time and fewer near falls. Secondary subgroup findings suggested different responses by disease severity. (low confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: For stairs, the Parkinson’s Foundation recommends clear, non-skid, well-lit steps and handrails; it advises avoiding ladders, step stools and chairs for climbing because balance and protective reflex changes increase fall risk. (low confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: The Cochrane review found a smaller probable reduction in the number of people experiencing at least one fall (risk ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.80–1.00), while effects on fall-related fractures and adverse events remained uncertain. (low confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: The 2022 Cochrane review found that exercise probably reduces fall rate in mild to moderate PD by 26% (rate ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.63–0.87; 1456 participants, 12 studies; moderate-certainty evidence). This describes falls per unit time, rather than a 26% reduction in the number of people who fall. (low confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: Home exercise benefits cannot be assumed to extend unchanged to severe PD. PDSAFE and a separate minimally supervised exercise trial found severity-dependent responses; in the latter, the higher-severity subgroup had a nonsignificant trend toward more falls. Subgroup findings warrant caution rather than a claim that exercise invariably harms advanced PD. (medium confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: The Parkinson’s Foundation recommends removing clutter and trip hazards, maintaining stable non-skid floors, improving lighting, creating wide walking paths, and keeping electrical cords out of walking routes. These are practical recommendations, rather than a quantified PD-specific intervention effect. (low confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: In the PDSAFE randomized trial, repeat falling at six months did not significantly improve: 61.5% in the intervention group versus 55% in controls (controlled OR 1.21, 95% CI 0.74–1.98). Balance, falls efficacy and chair stand time improved despite the negative primary fall outcome. (low confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: Exercise benefits should not be assumed to apply uniformly across PD severity: the Cochrane exercise evidence predominantly concerned mild to moderate disease, and PDSAFE subgroup analyses associated the intervention with an increased fall rate in the most severe group. The subgroup finding is a caution rather than proof that all exercise harms advanced PD. (medium confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: The APTA guideline strongly recommends physical-therapist-delivered balance training to improve postural control, balance, gait, mobility, balance confidence and quality of life. These outcomes should be distinguished from a demonstrated reduction in falls. (low confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: Practical PD home-safety guidance recommends clearing clutter and loose rugs, keeping cords out of walking routes, providing good lighting and leaving wide paths for mobility aids. These are guidance recommendations; these pages do not establish a PD-specific numerical treatment effect. (medium confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: Bathroom safety guidance recommends properly anchored grab bars, seated bathing options, better lighting and clear routes. Towel racks and similar fixtures should not be used as grab bars. (medium confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: The Parkinson’s Foundation recommends discussing an in-home occupational-therapy Home Safety Evaluation with the doctor to obtain personalized recommendations. (low confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: Mobility-aid selection should involve qualified professionals and assessment of the individual’s physical, attention and executive-function abilities. Evidence remains insufficient to identify a universally best PD walking aid. (medium confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: A walking aid does not necessarily reduce freezing. A small comparative study found that both standard and wheeled walkers slowed walking, the standard walker increased freezing and a laser attachment added no benefit; a systematic review likewise found limited and heterogeneous evidence for mobility aids. (medium confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: External cueing can improve freezing and gait outcomes, but those improvements should not be equated with proven fall prevention. The APTA guideline recommends cueing yet reports no studies of cueing effects on fall rate or number of falls in its evidence review; the mobility-aid review calls for more free-living controlled studies. (medium confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: The Parkinson’s Foundation advises planning how to call a family member or emergency services after a fall, including discussion of assistive technology with the doctor and occupational therapist. (low confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: In a Parkinson’s UK forum discussion, a participant described the importance of rollator brakes for public transport and handle-height adjustment. This is user experience that can inform assessment questions, not comparative evidence that a brand prevents falls. (low confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: For bathrooms, the Parkinson’s Foundation recommends grab bars near the toilet, tub and shower, an elevated toilet seat with support, and a sturdy shower or tub bench; towel racks and faucets should not serve as grab bars. (low confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: The Parkinson’s Foundation recommends accessible bedroom lighting and a nightlight for the route to the bathroom, and planning how to summon help after a fall. (low confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD

text: A 2022 mobility-aid review reported that some studies of canes and standard or two-wheeled walkers without visual cues found slower gait and shorter strides without significant improvement in freezing or falls. Visual or auditory cues improved some gait and freezing measures, but this does not establish reliable real-world fall prevention. (low confidence)
keywords: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
